  relationship_status: Married

  trauma_type: Terrorism

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Avoid Crowds: Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Vignette:
Kofi Mensah is a 78-year-old Ghanaian-born man who has worked for the past fourteen years as a librarian at a mid-sized public library in a mid-Atlantic city, where he and his wife of fifty-one years share a quiet house not far from the branch where he works. He came to the United States decades ago, built a life of deliberate orderliness, and had, by his own account, always taken a certain pride in his composure. That composure was shattered approximately three years ago when he was present at a public civic ceremony — a community anniversary celebration held in an outdoor plaza — during which a coordinated bombing attack killed several people and wounded dozens more. Kofi had been standing near the edge of the crowd when the first device detonated. He remembers with excruciating clarity the specific sequence of sensory details: the percussion of the blast moving through his chest before the sound fully registered, a child's red balloon drifting upward through a sudden column of grey smoke, the sight of people running in every direction while others lay motionless on the pavement. He was physically unharmed, but he remained on the scene for nearly an hour while emergency services responded, and what he witnessed during that time has not left him.

In the weeks that followed, Kofi found that the memory did not behave as memories were supposed to. It did not recede or soften. Instead it remained with a vivid, almost photographic completeness — the colour of the smoke, the particular angle of afternoon light, the expressions on faces he had never known. He described it in an early session as feeling less like remembering and more like being handed a film reel that runs on its own schedule. The replay arrives without his consent and without predictable cause. He has been in the library reshelfing periodicals when a patron dropped a heavy reference volume, and the sound returned him instantly and completely to the plaza. He was not reminded of the event; he was, for a moment, back inside it. This quality of ambush — the sense that the past can reclaim the present without warning — has become one of the most disorienting features of his daily life.

His occupation has not spared him. The library, which he once experienced as a place of refuge, has become a landscape of potential triggers. When patrons speak loudly, argue over computers, or behave in ways he considers disrespectful of the shared space, something tightens in him that goes beyond ordinary irritation. He had come to believe, though he struggled to articulate it precisely, that disorder and disregard for others carried a moral weight he could no longer treat as minor — as though the attack had permanently altered his threshold for what human carelessness meant. Certain conversations among colleagues or patrons — anything touching on public safety, bombings, political violence, or even loud public gatherings — can stop him mid-task. He has learned to excuse himself to the back office when such topics arise, and his colleagues have noticed an aloofness they cannot account for.

As the first anniversary of the attack approached, Kofi found himself unable to sleep for days beforehand. The date on the calendar felt less like a marker of time passed and more like a recurring wound. He has since structured his life in the months surrounding that anniversary with particular care, declining invitations and reducing his hours at the library during that period. More broadly, he has withdrawn from anything that might generate genuine pleasure or hope — family gatherings, a grandchild's birthday party, a church celebration his wife wanted to attend together. He could not explain to her, or fully to himself, why the prospect of happiness felt dangerous, only that it did. He has also stopped accompanying her to the grocery store, the farmers' market, any place where people gather in numbers. When the weight of it all becomes too heavy, he retreats into a kind of internal distance — sitting in his armchair in a state his wife describes as absent, present in the room but unreachable.

It was his wife who finally insisted he speak to someone. Kofi came to the first session quietly determined and quietly terrified — hoping, he said, that someone might help him understand why a man his age, who had survived so much, could be so thoroughly undone by something he had not even been meant to survive.
